description:
Courtship concerns the whole Christian community. Wesam Saad opens the course by addressing single adults, parents and older church members, explaining why preparation for marriage should begin before a young person seeks a spouse. He challenges the assumption that choosing and pursuing a marriage partner is an entirely private matter. Families and fellow believers have a part in offering guidance, and parents need clarity about what they are preparing their children to do. The session gathers questions about readiness, parental involvement, engagement, physical boundaries, doctrinal differences and online relationships, establishing the concerns that later studies will address.

Saad then sketches his account of changing Western marriage practices, moving from arranged marriages through courtship to modern dating. He describes courtship as directed towards marriage, involving family oversight while recognising the prospective couple’s consent. His overview contrasts that approach with relationships driven by private gratification and detached from family accountability. The historical outline introduces questions rather than settling every practical detail. Listeners are urged to examine inherited assumptions with an open mind and consider the biblical basis for their decisions. The course aims to develop constructive guidance, including how modern tools might be used without compromising purity and holiness.

questions.question: Why does the opening study address parents and older church members as well as single adults?
questions.answer: Saad presents preparation for marriage as a responsibility that begins before a young person is ready to marry. Parents need a clear direction for teaching their children, while older believers can offer guidance to those entering this stage of life. The course therefore concerns the wider church community.

questions.question: What assumption about choosing a spouse does Saad challenge?
questions.answer: He challenges the idea that the decision concerns only the two individuals and is nobody else’s business. He argues that marriage has a community dimension and that families and fellow believers have a legitimate role in guidance and discernment. The precise limits of those roles are questions for later sessions.

questions.question: Why does the teacher begin by collecting the group’s questions?
questions.answer: He wants to understand the listeners’ concerns and make sure the course addresses them carefully. Marriage decisions have a significant effect on people’s lives, so he intends to take time with the subject. Questions about boundaries, readiness, family disagreement and different circumstances become an agenda, rather than conclusions already established in this session.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the historical overview?
questions.answer: Saad uses his account of Western marriage practices to show that present customs are not the only possible model. He wants listeners to examine how familiar assumptions developed and to consider courtship without dismissing it simply because it is unfamiliar. The overview introduces the course’s later comparison of practices with Scripture.

questions.question: How does the introductory outline distinguish courtship from a marriage imposed on an unwilling person?
questions.answer: In Saad’s outline, family involvement does not remove the prospective husband’s or wife’s consent. He describes the transition from arrangements controlled by family authority to a courtship model that recognises the couple’s ability to refuse. He postpones a fuller explanation of how that process should work.

questions.question: Which priorities does Saad associate with courtship in this first session?
questions.answer: He presents courtship as a process directed towards marriage, with family involvement and an intention to preserve sexual purity. He also introduces caution about emotional attachment before commitment. These are opening principles whose reasons and practical implications he says he will unpack later.

questions.question: What constructive aim accompanies the criticism of modern dating?
questions.answer: Saad says the purpose is not merely to criticise dating. He wants to establish godly ways of pursuing marriage and to consider practical questions, including whether modern applications can be used as tools while preserving purity and holiness. Listeners are asked to remain open to examining their assumptions.
